transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-09-26
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Perez (Redwood SE), Liam Ross (Cobalt Maritime CTO), Priya Singh (Head of ML), Jamal Reyes (Infra Lead)

Auto-summary (auto):
- Customer is evaluating hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for low-latency streaming endpoints and high concurrency token throughput (p95 targets and steady-state tokens/sec).
- Primary concerns: p95 <= 150ms for short responses, streaming stability for long generates, predictable cost at scale, data residency and KMS integration for telemetry and request logs.
- Next step: shared pricing/SLAs + 24h benchmark with sample prompts.

Topics detected: hosting modes, p95 targets, concurrency, streaming token/sec, KV cache/ batching, autoscale, security (SOC2/KMS/VPC).

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Carlos from our SE team is here as well. How are we all?
[00:07] Liam Ross: Good, thanks. Excited to get into the latency stuff. We've got Priya and Jamal on too.
[00:12] Priya Singh: Hi, yeah thanks. We mostly want to understand p95 behaviour for short queries and token/sec for streaming, plus the hosting tradeoffs.
[00:19] Carlos Perez: Great. Quick agenda — 1) current infra + traffic patterns 2) p95 and streaming SLOs, 3) benchmark and deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private), 4) next steps. Sound ok?
[00:28] Jamal Reyes: Yep. We'll keep it focused. Sorry if I jump in with infra questions.
[00:31] Liam Ross: Perfect. So first, stack: our inference front end is in GCP europe-west1, we run a node fleet, and we use an internal cache layer. Production qps is around 40 req/s right now with spikes up to 250 req/s during events. Typical prompt lengths: 30–80 tokens for short replies, but we also have a few flows that stream 800–2k tokens.
[00:51] Priya Singh: Our hard p95 goal for short responses is 150ms end-to-end, and for streaming we want steady token emission with p95 between 200–400ms for the token arrival gap. Cost is also a major factor — we can't exceed X on variable TCO but we didn't give you that number yet.
[01:14] Carlos Perez: Right. Two quick clarifications: when you say p95 150ms, is that server-side CPU/gpu inference latency or end-to-end including network + front end?
[01:23] Liam Ross: End-to-end, from our API edge to first token.
[01:26] Carlos Perez: Good to know. Hosted mode generally gives lowest time-to-value but variable p95 because of multi-tenant queuing. Dedicated gives more predictable p95 and autoscale profiles we can tune. Private gives full network control but obviously more ops.
[01:41] Priya Singh: For Dedicated, do you guarantee p95 in the SLA? We need something we can show the board.
[01:47] Maya Chen: Our Dedicated slab — sorry, SLA — includes uptime and latency targets we can commit to per contract. We typically commit to a p95 tail for a given model class and request shape; we'll send the exact numbers for the model family you care about.
[01:58] Jamal Reyes: Important: we need VPC peering and KMS. We can't send raw logs outside our VPC, and audit trails must land in our own SIEM.
[02:06] Carlos Perez: Understood — Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM integrations; Dedicated supports VPC options with encrypted logs. We'll share the SOC2, encryption at rest and in transit details.
[02:17] Liam Ross: Ok. On the p95 details, we want to simulate our traffic shape: 60% short single-token or short-generation requests, 30% mid (200–600 tokens), 10% long streaming sessions. How do you model batching and KV cache impact on p95?
[02:33] Carlos Perez: Two levers: continuous batching and KV/prefix caching. For short requests, batching increases throughput but can raise latency if you wait for batch windows. We recommend very small batch sizes or adaptive latency budgets for p95-critical routes. Also, prefix caching reduces compute for repeated contexts — that can drop p95 significantly if you have heavy prefix reuse.
[02:53] Maya Chen: Quick note, when folks hear KV cache they sometimes see K-V cash in transcripts, hah — we actually saw that in an earlier call.
[02:59] Priya Singh: Ha. Yeah we do reuse prompts heavily in a support flow so caching could help.
[03:04] Carlos Perez: For streaming, our runtime supports progressive token emission with low per-token overhead. The token/sec steady-state depends on model size, quantization, and batch mixing — with 8-bit quant you'll get faster per-token emission in many cases.
[03:17] Liam Ross: Do you support per-request quantization profiles? We have a few models where quality matters.
[03:22] Carlos Perez: Yes, you can pin quantization profiles per model variant. For critical quality routes we keep FP16 or higher and tune autoscale. For lower-stakes paths, 4-bit or 8-bit quantization saves cost.
[03:33] Liam Ross: What's the expected p95 improvement with KV cache on short replies? Any ballpark numbers?
[03:37] Carlos Perez: Ballpark — if you have high prefix reuse, KV cache can reduce compute by 30–60% on the repeated portion. For p95 you'll often drop 20–40% depending on network overhead. I'll put concrete numbers in the benchmark matrix.
[03:51] Priya Singh: Benchmark — we want a 24h run that recreates spikes. Can the Redwood SE run that for us or do you want our VPC access?
[03:58] Maya Chen: We can run it on Redwood Dedicated or Hosted environments with a signed test plan. For Private, we'd need your infra access. Carlos, thoughts?
[04:06] Carlos Perez: We typically run an SE-led benchmark on Dedicated to get representative p95 and tokens/sec. For Private, we do a joint run. We'll need your sample prompt set, distribution, and a small sample corpus.
[04:17] Jamal Reyes: We'll produce traffic profiles and a secure S3 link for prompts. Security-wise, we want logs pushed to our SIEM via a web hook inside the VPC. Can Redwood support that?
[04:27] Carlos Perez: Yes, we can set up log forwarding to your SIEM with encryption in transit and per-tenant keying. For Hosted, we maintain the control plane, but logs can be exported per contract.
[04:36] Liam Ross: About concurrency: our spike behavior is bursts of 200–250 req/s for 2–10 minutes. How does dedicated sizing work for that?
[04:44] Carlos Perez: Dedicated sizing is capacity-based. We compute tokens/sec demand at peak, factor in average token length and model token/sec on chosen instance types, and add headroom for autoscale. Example — if your peaks are 250 req/s with avg 50 tokens, that's 12.5k tokens/sec required. On a cGPU instance family you might get 6–8k tokens/sec depending on model size, so you'd provision two replicas plus autoscale to handle concurrency. We'll prepare a sizing table.
[05:09] Priya Singh: That math checks out. Can you also show cold start behaviour? One fear is that autoscale spin-up hurts p95 during event bursts.
[05:18] Carlos Perez: Yes — we can show cold start numbers and recommend warm pools and burst capacity. For Dedicated we can keep a small warm pool which reduces cold start latency to single-digit ms for model KV load, but there's still some first-request overhead.
[05:30] Maya Chen: Also worth noting we have multi-region fallback. If europe-west1 has a transient issue, we can route to europe-west2 with slight added latency; that helps availability for events.
[05:38] Liam Ross: Hmm, for regulatory reasons we need EU-only. But multi-region within EU is fine.
[05:42] Priya Singh: On cost, how do you display token-level cost and where can we see hot routes?
[05:47] Carlos Perez: Redwood Console shows token-level cost, per-route latency breakdown and heatmaps. We'll give you a demo link.
[05:52] Liam Ross: Good. A concrete ask from procurement: we need a p95 guarantee for the short response model under Dedicated with a defined Fallback policy if threshold exceeded. Do you do canary rollouts and A/B?
[06:03] Maya Chen: Yes, rollouts and canaries are first-class. You can define fallback to a cheaper model variant or another region automatically when latency or errors cross a threshold. We'll include a sample policy.
[06:13] Jamal Reyes: For Private, how hands-on is the install? Would ops be able to run the on-prem package?
[06:18] Carlos Perez: The on-prem package is an appliance + control plane that you manage. We'll provide deploy docs, Helm charts for k8s installs, and a runbook. For air-gapped environments we have an offline bundle.
[06:29] Priya Singh: Ok. For the benchmark, what metrics will you capture? We want p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, per-token latency, memory and GPU utilization, queue depths.
[06:39] Carlos Perez: We'll capture all that plus KV hit rates, batch size distributions, and tracing for first-byte and last-byte timings. We'll publish a CSV and dashboards.
[06:49] Liam Ross: On competitors — we've looked at ModelX and NimbusAI. ModelX advertised low p95 but we saw token-emission jitter in streaming. Curious how Redwood handles deterministic token emission.
[07:00] Carlos Perez: Our runtime prioritizes steady token emission by avoiding large batch mixing on streaming routes; we can pin a route to non-batching policy to keep per-token jitter low.
[07:09] Maya Chen: Also the billing model — we charge per-token for Hosted and per-token + capacity for Dedicated; for Private it's a license plus infra costs. We'll send a pricing sheet.
[07:18] Priya Singh: Can we get an estimate for steady-state cost at 12.5k tokens/sec?
[07:23] Maya Chen: We'll include a cost model in the deliverables — rough estimate in the sheet and a more precise number after the 24h run.
[07:30] Jamal Reyes: One more technical: do you support HSM-backed KMS keys for encryption at rest and for log signing?
[07:36] Carlos Perez: Yes, HSM integrations are supported in Private and Dedicated with enterprise add-on. We'll include the integration doc.
[07:44] Liam Ross: Great. Let's discuss the test plan briefly. We'll provide a traffic file: 70% short, 20% mid, 10% long streaming. We want both steady runs and spike windows at 4x baseline for 10 minutes to emulate event traffic. Can you run both?
[07:59] Carlos Perez: Yes, we'll run the baseline 24h and a focused spike harness. We'll capture per-route p95 during spikes.
[08:07] Priya Singh: How do you simulate networking latency from our edge? We want realistic e2e numbers.
[08:12] Carlos Perez: Ideally we run the test from your edge or a colocated test runner with a one-way latency shim to match your front-end. For Hosted/Dedicated we can inject latency in the runner to match your observed numbers. For Private we do the run inside your network if you give access.
[08:27] Liam Ross: Ok. Can you give an example of a past benchmark? We want a template.
[08:31] Carlos Perez: Sure — I can attach a benchmark report from a previous retail customer where we achieved p95 of 120ms for short responses on Dedicated with warm pools and 3x headroom for spikes; streaming token emission was ~12ms per token at steady state on quantized model. I'll anonymize it.
[08:46] Maya Chen: We'll share that report plus a sizing matrix.
[08:50] (brief crosstalk)
[08:52] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[08:55] Priya Singh: On SLAs, if you miss p95, what's the penalty? Procurement needs the remedy terms.
[09:02] Maya Chen: Remedy terms are standard credits or extended term options; specifics will be in the contract. We'll have legal coordinate with your procurement team.
[09:10] Jamal Reyes: We'll need a data processing addendum — who's the data processor?
[09:14] Carlos Perez: Redwood is the processor for Hosted; for Dedicated/Private we can be a processor or you can be controller depending on setup — we'll send the DPA.
[09:24] Liam Ross: Ok good. Any gotchas on multi-tenant hosted p95?
[09:28] Carlos Perez: Hosted is multi-tenant so we do more aggressive packing; for p95-sensitive routes we often recommend Dedicated. However, some customers accept slight variability in exchange for lower ops.
[09:39] Priya Singh: For our board, the order of preference is Dedicated first, Private second if needed for compliance. Hosted as a fallback for dev.
[09:47] Maya Chen: That helps. We'll tailor the proposal around Dedicated with a Private option.
[09:52] Liam Ross: Cool. Logistics: timeline — we want the benchmark and pricing within two weeks, and procurement would like to get pricing by end of month.
[09:59] Maya Chen: We'll target sending pricing and SOW by 2028-09-28 and schedule the benchmark for the week of 2028-10-03.
[10:06] Carlos Perez: I'll put together the benchmark matrix and a runbook and send it to Priya and Jamal after the call.
[10:13] Priya Singh: Sounds good. Quick question — do you expose per-request trace IDs so we can correlate with our logs?
[10:19] Carlos Perez: Yes, we can add trace IDs and full trace hooks. We'll show how to correlate in the runbook.
[10:27] Liam Ross: Ok wrapping up. Anything else?
[10:30] Maya Chen: Just to recap and to be explicit on next steps: 1) Maya will send Dedicated pricing + SLA and the anonymized benchmark report by 2028-09-28, 2) Carlos will send benchmark matrix and runbook and propose a bench date (2028-10-03 window), 3) Cobalt to send sample prompts, traffic profile and S3 link by 2028-09-29, 4) Redwood to schedule SE bench and share SOC2/KMS docs.
[10:52] Priya Singh: That matches. Priya here will own the prompt/traffic deliverable.
[10:56] Jamal Reyes: I'll coordinate with Priya on S3 and VPC details.
[10:59] Liam Ross: Procurement will expect the pricing sheet and SOW. I'll be in copy.
[11:04] Maya Chen: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the attachments.
[11:09] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional overlaps, some technical terms were auto-corrected (e.g., K-V cash -> KV cache, slab -> SLA).
